messages.author: 5900eadecec2d82d
messages.subject: ADMIN: No attachments
parts:
Could I remind everyone on the distance-sampling list to please refrain from
enclosing attachments with their messages. This is standard netiquette, and
is also outlined in the list guidelines, which are sent to all new members
when they subsribe, and are available on the web at
http://www.mailbase.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling/ (under Introduction)
Please ignore the rest of this message if you are already aware of this.

Thanks!

- Len Thomas
distance-sampling list admin

Why shouldn't I send attachments?
---------------------------------

1. Remember that your message gets passed on to several hundred other people,
some of whom may not have high-speed access to the internet and others who
may not have mail spoolers with large capacities. By sending a large
attachment without their prior consent, you risk crashing some people's mail
systems.

2. Many of the people on the list will not be interested in your particular
question, so will not want to see the dataset/screengrab you are posting.
This is frustrating for them if they spent many minutes downloading your
message down a 'phone line.

3. Many mail reading programs cannot deal with attachments, and your message
shows up on such systems as a seemingly random series of ASCII text.

What should I do instead?
-------------------------

1. If you have an anonymous ftp server at your site, upload your
picture/dataset to it (*zipped up* to make it more compact and easier to
transport) and include details of how to download the file inside your
*text only* message for those who are interested.

2. If you have a web server, the easiest thing for pictures is to put them on
your server and provide the URL (web address) in your message.

3. If you have none of these, offer to email the file to anyone who asks you
for it. You will be surprised how few people do! However, this way, you can
be sure that it will reach those who are interested.

These things take more time on your part, but people (such as me) will thank
you for your politeness!



--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland KY16 9SS

email: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk
